signals.title: AWS Reports MoE Inference Gains on SageMaker | ToolboxKart
signals.excerpt:
AWS reports up to 10% more throughput and 9% faster first-token latency from three MoE kernel changes on H200 GPUs. See what changed and the main limits.
...
AWS published three kernel optimizations for mixture-of-experts (MoE) model serving on Amazon SageMaker AI on October 13, 2026. The company reports up to 10% higher end-to-end throughput and up to 9% faster time to first token on NVIDIA H200 GPUs across the optimizations it describes. The changes target GPU matrix layout, the backend used for FP8 quantized models and unnecessary Triton just-in-time compilations.

These are specific engineering results, not a promise that every MoE model will become 10% faster. The gains depend on the model, quantization, batch size, serving stack and the bottleneck in the current deployment. AWS presents the results from its own implementation and testing.
...
| Change | Target | AWS-reported result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Swap-AB for WGMMA | Improve matrix tile use during thin decode batches | About 2–4% higher end-to-end output throughput in the reported large-scale MoE tests on H200 |
| FP8 backend routing | Route FP8 tensor-quantized fused MoE work to Triton instead of the default FlashInfer/CUTLASS path | About 10% higher end-to-end throughput in the reported H200 workload |
| Remove unnecessary Triton JIT recompilation | Avoid recompiling a variable-length kernel for each new token count | About 9% faster time to first token on H200 at eight-way tensor parallelism |
...
The Swap-AB change transposes the multiplication so the large expert dimension occupies the operand position that benefits from the hardware layout. AWS says this improves tile utilization and asynchronous prefetching, producing a 2–4% end-to-end output-throughput gain in its large-scale MoE tests on H200. The optimization was upstreamed to vLLM and is available in vLLM 0.24.0 or later, according to the AWS post.
...
The second change concerns FP8 tensor-quantized fused MoE models. AWS says profiling showed that the Triton backend outperformed the default FlashInfer/CUTLASS path in the low-concurrency Hopper workloads it examined. Its routing policy now selects Triton for that case.

The point is not that Triton is always faster than CUTLASS. Kernel backends behave differently across hardware, quantization formats, token counts and concurrency levels. AWS reports a 10% end-to-end throughput improvement for the FP8 quantized fused MoE workload it tested on H200. The change is available in the AWS Large Model Inference container version 28, according to the post.
...
The third optimization addresses Triton JIT compilation. Triton can specialize a kernel for integer arguments. If a serving workload passes a new value for a specialized argument, the runtime may compile another kernel variant. AWS found that the variable token count in the fused rotary-position-embedding and FP8-quantization kernel was causing repeated compilation.

The team marked variable-length parameters so Triton would not specialize on them. AWS says that removed the repeated compilations and improved time to first token by 9% on H200 at eight-way tensor parallelism. The change was upstreamed to vLLM 0.22.0 or later.
...
Start with the current serving container, vLLM version, GPU type, quantization format and model architecture. Record them before changing a kernel or backend. If the deployment uses a managed SageMaker container, verify the exact image version rather than assuming that a new upstream change is already present.
...
The reported percentages do not establish a universal speedup for every MoE model or every H200 deployment. The post focuses on particular kernel paths and test configurations. It also does not mean that a serving team can ignore batching, memory use, request scheduling or the cost of keeping GPUs underused while models load.
...

signals.title: Muse Wonder | Meta AI Research
signals.excerpt:
Today, we’re excited to introduce the Muse Wonder series with Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, our most capable models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence. Muse Wonder brings together Active Memory and Active Focus to keep track of what matters to you and work diligently toward what you want to accomplish.

Muse Wonder is available today through the Meta Model API and Muse Code, and Muse Wonder Full is available today for Muse Code subscribers.
...
When we introduced Muse Spark, we outlined our approach to predictable, rigorous scaling. Today’s release builds on that work across pretraining and reinforcement learning, delivering our most capable models yet. Trained at our gigawatt-scale Prometheus data center, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full bring together the work of teams across Meta to deliver frontier capabilities for complex tasks at work and in everyday life — another step toward bringing personal superintelligence to the billions of people who use our products.
...
The Muse Wonder series achieves state-of-the-art results across key benchmarks for personal and professional agents, memory, and coding.

The full results below compare Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full with other frontier models across a broad evaluation suite.
...
The results above provide a broad view of the models’ performance. We now take a closer look at four areas central to their work on real-world tasks: domain expertise, Active Memory, Active Focus, and frontier coding.
...
Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full apply specialized knowledge to problems people encounter at work and in daily life, from understanding a lease to making sense of financial or health information. Our evaluations include tasks in law, finance, and health that test this ability. Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), for example, requires models to work with source documents and follow detailed instructions to produce legal work products.
...
One of the most critical steps towards useful personal and professional agents is reliable memory. Models need to remember what matters and recognize when earlier information becomes relevant. We call this Active Memory: carrying important context about you across conversations and actively retrieving the details relevant to the task at hand.
...
Using that context to complete a task also requires sustained effort. Active Focus describes how Muse Wonder continues working toward a challenging goal: trying alternative approaches, working through blockers, and adapting to new information. Along the way, it asks for clarification when needed and checks in before taking important actions. We evaluate focus through FocusBench and sustained execution through SWE-Marathon, which tests work on long-running software projects.
...
Coding brings these capabilities together. Building software requires tracking requirements, making changes across a codebase, and working through repeated cycles of testing and revision. Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full deliver frontier coding performance, supporting projects from small applications to complex software. We trained both models on diverse, long-running tasks to help them sustain progress across this process.
...
Two models often have similar benchmark scores, yet one seems to handle a much wider range of unfamiliar tasks. That’s what complaints of “benchmaxxing” and praise for “big model smell” both get at: a breadth of capability that popular benchmarks in a few domains can’t fully capture.

To quantify this mismatch, we investigate how performance on tasks targeted during post-training relates to performance on unfamiliar tasks as we scale test-time compute. The plot below compares Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Wonder Full, with each point denoting performance at a distinct reasoning effort. The horizontal axis shows the model’s score on a composite representative of the tasks we focused on during post-training (“in-distribution”). The vertical axis shows the average score on a set of tasks we did not target during post-training (“out-of-distribution”).

Both of our models improve similarly on out-of-distribution tasks as we scale test-time compute. But given its in-distribution performance, Muse Wonder Full performs even better on unfamiliar tasks than the Muse Spark 1.3 trend would predict. This upward shift is because Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full build on larger, stronger base models: a stronger base yields post-training gains that carry over more effectively to unfamiliar tasks. That versatility especially matters for personal agents, which need to handle many combinations of goals, tools, and constraints — not all of which we can anticipate during training.
...
Delivering personal superintelligence to everyone requires a significant investment in alignment and safety. A personal agent takes actions on a user’s behalf and might handle context such as messages, calendars, and private documents. That level of access demands a model that exercises discretion with private information and resists misuse. We trained the Muse Wonder family to lead on both dimensions, with robustness to adversarial instructions and careful handling of private information.

As models become more capable, our goal is to help people harness those capabilities safely and responsibly. Muse Wonder offers our strongest safeguards to date against CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear) and cyber misuse, while preserving access to frontier cyber capabilities for defensive use, per our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework.

Muse Wonder is our most aligned model to date, and alignment is central to how we build personal superintelligence. A full report with additional safety evaluations will be available soon.

The 16-bit Qwen3.8 Flash Next checkpoint is 360 GB. Two Radeon AI PRO R9700 cards offer 64 GB of VRAM between them, so the original model is far out of reach. Our new 4-bit release runs on those two cards, with results close to the 16-bit reference on math, Python coding and knowledge tasks. 1

# SGLang and Miles on NVIDIA Vera Rubin

We had early access to two NVIDIA Vera Rubin nodes (8 GPUs) and used them to bring SGLang and Miles up on the platform: SGLang for inference and Miles for RL training. On the inference side, we tuned SGLang for Kimi K3 NVFP4: this post covers what we changed in the attention, MoE/communication and KDA kernels, and how much each change bought. On the training side, Miles, which uses SGLang for rollout and Megatron for training, runs RL end to end on Vera Rubin out of the box, including agentic RL with sandboxes on the Vera CPU.

NVIDIA Vera Rubin is the GPU generation after NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra (GB300 NVL72). For kernel work, the most impactful changes are more shared memory per CTA (327 KiB, up from the 227 KiB on NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell), more SMs (212 on our nodes), and NVIDIA NVLink 6. Some of our changes retune Blackwell-era kernels for these new limits. The rest remove overheads we found while profiling Kimi K3 on Rubin, such as kernel launches, barrier stalls and hidden copies.

Cognition has deployed Vera Rubin NVL72 with its own SGLang-based stack and has reported up to a 4.8x increase in total token throughput over GB200 NVL72. 1

Kimi K3 is a 2.8T-parameter hybrid model with a 1M-token context window. Its 93 attention layers interleave 69 KDA linear-attention layers with 24 MLA layers, and every attention output is banked and aggregated per block through Attention Residuals. The FFN is a LatentMoE with 896 experts, top-16 routing, running in a 3584-dimensional latent space. We serve the NVFP4 checkpoint with RadixArk's DSpark block speculative decoding, so every decode step is a short draft pass followed by a verify pass over the drafted tokens.

Over a window of *L* tokens, conventional decoding reads the state *L* times and writes it *L* times. ReplaySSM still reads the checkpoint on every step, because the output needs it, but writes it only once, during the flush. A non-flush step has one job—computing the output—and writes only the new input record, a few vectors instead of a full matrix. This roughly halves the dominant state traffic.
At serving batch sizes, memory bandwidth limits the conventional kernel’s performance, so reducing state memory traffic speeds up decoding. At batch size 1, other sources of latency dominate, and ReplaySSM provides no speedup in these tests. **LFM2.5-24B-A2B** is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

## How we built a reasoning agent with 2B active parameters
LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

1. **Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)**
2. **Teacher specialization**
3. **Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD), non-agentic:** distill the specialist teachers on non-agentic tasks.
4. **MOPD, agentic:** a second distillation stage focused on agentic tasks.

signals.excerpt:
ColGrep-Agent-2B moves repository exploration to a small local model. Its reported benchmark highlights a useful design pattern—and the accuracy, latency and evaluation questions teams should examine before adopting it.
...
Delegating repository exploration to a local specialist can compress context, but teams should validate retrieval coverage, end-to-end accuracy, latency and total compute on their own codebases.

Coding assistants do not spend all their tokens writing code. A substantial share can disappear into repository navigation: searching for an unfamiliar concept, opening likely files, tracing references and then carrying those observations through later turns. LightOn's ColGrep-Agent-2B release targets that exploration loop with a small model running beside the developer's main coding agent. The important idea is broader than one tool: expensive reasoning models do not necessarily need to perform every retrieval step themselves.

The release describes a 2-billion-parameter local agent layered on ColGrep's semantic code search. It can search, read files and return paths, line ranges and relevant code to a larger coding assistant. In the authors' evaluation, Claude Code handled 52 code-search questions across 13 repositories, with three runs in four search configurations. The fully delegated setup reportedly used 34.3% fewer API tokens than built-in grep, while observed correct-answer rates were 80.8% and 83.3% respectively. The authors correctly note that the accuracy difference was not statistically significant, but its confidence interval was wide enough to include a meaningful decline. These are code-location questions, not complete software-engineering tasks.
...
A specialized search agent changes the interface. Instead of exposing every exploratory step, it accepts a behavior-level question and returns a compact evidence bundle. If that bundle contains the right locations and enough surrounding code, the main agent can start reasoning from evidence rather than from a blank map. The savings therefore come from context compression as much as from better retrieval. Compute has not vanished; some of it has moved to a local model whose tokens are outside the hosted model's billing and context loop.

That distinction matters when comparing systems. A lower API-token count is not automatically lower total cost. Teams should also count local inference time, memory, index maintenance, installation overhead and the cost of bad retrieval. Privacy can improve because repository exploration stays local, but only if the entire indexing and inference path is operated as expected.
...
The evaluation offers a useful controlled comparison because the question and repository remain fixed while the search interface changes. Repeated runs and question-level confidence intervals are stronger evidence than a handful of favorable demonstrations. The reported “Balanced” configuration is especially informative: it matched grep's observed accuracy while saving 21.2% of tokens, suggesting that routing may be more robust than delegating every search.
...
The latency tradeoff is visible too. The delegated agent used fewer main-model turns but took longer per question in the reported aggregate. That may be acceptable for unattended work or costly hosted inference, and less attractive during rapid interactive debugging. Averages can also hide hardware sensitivity because local model speed depends on the available backend and memory.
...
Teams considering this pattern should assemble questions from their own completed issues rather than starting with synthetic prompts. Each question should name the user-visible behavior without revealing internal identifiers. Record the files and symbols a maintainer needed, then compare three modes: existing search tools, delegated semantic search and a hybrid router.

Score more than whether one expected file appears. Useful retrieval should cover every required location, avoid irrelevant context and provide enough neighboring code to support the next decision. Measure main-model input and output tokens, wall-clock time, local resource use and end-to-end task success. Review failures by type: missing an alias, stopping at an interface, overlooking configuration, or returning plausible but unrelated code. Those categories reveal whether tuning the index, prompt or routing policy is likely to help.

A safe rollout also preserves an escape hatch. The main agent should be able to fall back to literal search and direct file reads when delegated results are sparse or contradictory. For high-impact changes, returned line ranges are leads, not proof; the coding agent still needs to inspect current code, callers and tests. Read-only search permissions are a sensible default because a retrieval specialist does not need authority to modify the repository.
...
ColGrep-Agent-2B illustrates a modular agent architecture: assign a narrow, tool-heavy subproblem to a smaller local model and pass a compact result to the more capable model. The value depends less on parameter count than on a clean contract between the two layers. The specialist must return evidence that is concise, inspectable and easy to verify.

For coding tools, that contract can reduce repeated exploration without pretending retrieval is solved. The most credible adoption path is therefore incremental: benchmark on local questions, use hybrid routing, watch both accuracy and latency, and retain conventional search as a fallback. Token savings are valuable, but the real objective is reliable evidence per unit of time and compute.

A new Hugging Face paper introduces SoloQ, a calibration-free quantization framework for diffusion large language models that preserves accuracy at 4-bit precision and cuts peak memory by up to 2.61x.

- SoloQ retains accuracy under 4-bit quantization and beats calibration-based baselines on knowledge- and reasoning-intensive benchmarks across LLaDA, Dream, Fast-dLLM v2, and Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion.

...
Enter SoloQ, a calibration-free quantization framework from researchers publishing on Hugging Face. SoloQ maps weights and activations into a normalized rotated basis with a predictable marginal distribution, enabling data-independent quantization. It combines a structured K-RPBH rotation with a lightweight rescaling correction, and its predictable post-rotation distribution supports both distribution-matched codebooks and hardware-native NVFP4.

For block-diffusion models, SoloQ adds commit-time KV-cache quantization, compressing persistent states without disturbing the block currently being denoised.

Across full-sequence dLLMs (LLaDA and Dream) and block-diffusion dLLMs (Fast-dLLM v2 and Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion), SoloQ retains accuracy under 4-bit quantization and outperforms calibration-based baselines on knowledge- and reasoning-intensive benchmarks. With NVFP4, it reduces peak memory by up to 2.61x and accelerates end-to-end inference by up to 2.24x.
